# Phase 1: Blind analysis

## Experimental Design
RNA sequencing analysis was performed on 2 groups with 3 replicates per group numbered 1 to 3. For each of the six samples, there were R1 and R2, signifying paired-end sequencing. In our analysis, no covariates are provided and the only information provided is the condition and sample number. This experimental design supports the analysis of identifying differences between control and experimental samples. The three samples for each group provide better estimation for variability within each group. Certain effects are unable to be detected such as effects due to sex difference and small sample groups causing limited ability to detect changes in expression. Potential confounders would be if the batching of the samples were different such as library preparation date, biology if the sex or age are different, and if the sample quality was good or not, ie low sequencing depth or rna degradation. As no covariate information was provided, factors just discussed cannot be included in the DESeq2 model. These issues can only be checked partially by comparing sequencing depth and alignment rates across the samples in the MultiQC report and checking the PCA if the samples cluster by condition rather than by any other factor. 


## Methods


### RNA-seq preprocessing and Nextflow pipeline
RNA-seq data processing was performed using a custom Nextflow (v26.04.6) pipeline executed on the Boston University Shared Computing Cluster (BU SCC). The pipeline was run using containerized tools (Docker images from ghcr.io/bu-cds-bf528/*:latest, executed with Singularity). Six paired-end RNA-seq samples, consisting of three control and three experimental samples, were analyzed. The GRCh38 primary assembly reference genome and corresponding GENCODE v45 primary assembly gene annotation (GTF) were used for read alignment and quantification. Read quality was assessed using FastQC (v0.12.1) with default parameters on both forward (R1) and reverse (R2) reads for each sample. A genome index was generated using STAR (v2.7.11b) with the --runMode genomeGenerate and --sjdbGTFfile parameters to incorporate the GENCODE annotation; all other parameters were left at their defaults. Reads were subsequently aligned to the reference genome using STAR (v2.7.11b), with --readFilesCommand zcat for decompression of input FASTQ files and --outSAMtype BAM Unsorted for BAM output; all other alignment parameters were set to default values. Gene-level read counts were generated using VERSE (v0.1.5) with the -S option to accommodate paired-end alignments that were not sorted by read name and the GENCODE v45 GTF annotation. All other VERSE parameters were left at their default settings. Per-sample gene count files were combined into a gene-by-sample count matrix using a custom Python script with pandas (v3.0.1). Gene identifiers were subsequently mapped to gene names using a second custom Python script (run in a Biopython v1.86 container), extracting gene ID and gene name pairs from gene features in the GTF annotation. Finally, MultiQC (v1.33) was used with default parameters to aggregate FastQC reports and STAR Log.final.out alignment statistics into a consolidated quality control report.

### Differential expression and functional enrichment analysis
Downstream analyses were performed in R (v4.4.3) using DESeq2 (v1.46.0), tidyverse (v2.0.0; ggplot2 v3.5.1, dplyr v1.1.4, and readr v2.1.5), fgsea (v1.32.4), msigdbr (v7.5.1), and pheatmap (v1.0.12). Genes were filtered to retain those with at least 10 raw counts in at least three of the six samples. Differential gene expression between experimental and control conditions was assessed using DESeq2 with a design formula of ~ condition and a contrast of experimental versus control. Statistical significance was determined using the default Wald test, with p-values adjusted for multiple testing using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. Genes with an adjusted p-value (padj) below 0.05 were considered significantly differentially expressed and categorized as upregulated (log2 fold change > 0) or downregulated (log2 fold change < 0) in the experimental condition relative to the control. For sample-level quality control, counts were transformed using the variance-stabilizing transformation (VST) with blind = TRUE. Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed using DESeq2's plotPCA function, with samples visualized according to experimental condition. Additionally, a sample-to-sample Euclidean distance matrix was calculated from the transformed expression data and visualized using pheatmap. Functional overrepresentation analysis was conducted using the DAVID Functional Annotation Chart (accessed November 2, 2026), with upregulated and downregulated gene lists submitted separately as official gene symbols (Homo sapiens). All genes retained after count filtering were supplied as the background gene set. Default DAVID parameters were used (EASE score threshold = 0.1; minimum count = 2), and terms with Benjamini-adjusted p-values below 0.05 were considered significant. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was performed using fgsea with the Molecular Signatures Database (MSigDB) v7.5.1 C2 canonical pathways collection, retrieved using msigdbr (v7.5.1). Ensembl gene IDs were mapped to gene symbols, and genes with missing log2 fold-change values or duplicate symbols were removed; the remaining genes were ranked by log2 fold change. Enrichment analysis was performed with a minimum pathway size of 15, a maximum pathway size of 500, and a random seed of 42. Pathways with Benjamini-Hohberg-adjusted p-values below 0.05 were considered significantly enriched.

## Read Quality Control

Read quality was assessed using FastQC and summarized with MultiQC. Sequencing depth ranged from 84.5 million (control_rep2) to 118.9 million (control_rep3) read pairs across the six samples. FastQC flagged per-base sequence content as failing for all R1 files and as a warning for all R2 files. Sequence duplication levels were also flagged as failing across all twelve FASTQ files. These warnings do not necessarily indicate poor sequencing quality as elevated duplication levels are commonly observed in RNA-seq experiments because highly expressed transcripts generate many identical reads. Overrepresented sequences were flagged in six of the twelve FASTQ files (control_rep1 R1, control_rep3 R1 and R2, exp_rep2 R1 and R2, and exp_rep3 R1). However, the proportion of the reads corresponding to overrepresented sequences was minimal, with every FASTQ files containing less than 1% overrepresented sequences. Adapter contamination was also minimal across all samples, so adapter trimming was not performed. 

Alignment to the GRCh38 reference genome using STAR showed consistently high alignment rates across all six samples. Overall alignment rates, including both uniquely and multimapped reads, ranged from 95.8% (exp_rep2) to 97.8% (control_rep2). Uniquely mapped reads ranged from 91.9% (exp_rep3) to 94.0% (control_rep2), while reads mapped to multiple loci ranged from 3.7% (exp_rep2) to 4.9% (exp_rep3). Sequencing depth and alignment rates did not differ systematically between control and experimental samples as well. These results indicate that the majority of sequenced reads mapped successfully and uniquely to the reference genome, with relatively low multimapping rates. Given the high alignment rates, low multimapping, negligible adapter content, and FastQC warnings correlated with RNA-sequencing, the data were considered high quality and suitable for downstream analyses without additional read trimming or preprocessing.

## Filtering the Counts Matrix

Genes were filtered to keep only those with at least 10 raw counts in at least three of the six samples. Before filtering, the counts matrix contained 63,241 genes and after filtering, 20,579 genes were retained. Before filtering, the median log10(count + 1) values were near or at zero in every sample. This indicates that most of the genes had little to no detectable expression and the expressed genes appeared only as upper outliers. After filtering, median log10(count + 1) values were approximately 2.8 in all samples.

This filter follows the DESeq2 vignette's pre-filtering recommendation of at least 10 counts in at least as many samples as the smallest group. A threshold of 10 counts was used alongside a minimum of three samples being required because three is the size of each group, so a gene expressed in only one condition is still retained. At the sequencing depth (~85-119 million read pairs per sample), 10 counts corresponds to only about 0.1 count per million, so the filter chosen is quite lenient. It essentially removes the unexpressed genes and keeps genes with low expression.

```{r filter_counts}
# Filter the counts matrix
counts_filtered <- counts %>%
  filter(rowSums(across(-gene) >= 10) >= 3)
nrow(counts)
nrow(counts_filtered)
```

```{r counts_distribution_before}
# Plot the distribution of counts before filtering
counts_long <- counts %>% pivot_longer(-gene, names_to = "sample", values_to = "count")

ggplot(counts_long, aes( x = sample, y = log10(count+1))) +
  geom_boxplot() + 
  labs(title = "Counts before filtering",
       x = "Sample",
       y = "log10(count + 1)")
```

```{r counts_distribution_after}
# Plot the distribution of counts after filtering
counts_filtered_long <- counts_filtered %>% pivot_longer(-gene, names_to = "sample", values_to = "count")

ggplot(counts_filtered_long, aes( x = sample, y = log10(count+1))) +
  geom_boxplot() + 
  labs(title = "Counts after filtering",
       x = "Sample",
       y = "log10(count + 1)")
```

## Differential Expression Analysis

Differential Expression analysis was performed on the 20,579 genes, with 1,254 being significantly differentially expressed between the experimental and control groups at padj < 0.05. Of these genes, 572 were upregulated and 682 were downregulated in the experimental condition. The top-10 table created showcase that the most significant gene was RPS4Y1 with a log2FC of -8.8, with other top genes being lncRNAs or unannotated loci.

Upregulated and downregulated genes were submitted to DAVID separately. This was done so that results could be distinct between genes being upregulated and downregulated rather than diluted together. The background utilized was all 20,579 genes that passed filtering as these genes were the set that was used to detect the differentially expressed genes. DAVID recognized 415 of the 572 upregulated and 611 of the 682 downregulated genes. At Benjamini < 0.05, 153 terms were enriched among upregulated genes and 88 among downregulated genes. Upregulated genes were strongly enriched for secreted and extracellular proteins, including glycoprotein, extracellular region, secreted, and extracellular matrix among others. Downregulated genes were enriched for plasma membrane, synapse, nervous system development, developmental proteins, and immunoglobulin-like domains. These results suggest that the experimental condition increases expression of extracellular matrix and secretory functions while reducing nervous system and synaptic related genes.

Gene set enrichment analysis was performed using fgsea with MSigDB C2 canonical pathways, with genes ranked by log2 fold change; pathways with padj < 0.05 were considered significant. Positively enriched pathways were dominated by extracellular matrix organization, collagen formation, and signaling pathways. Negatively enriched pathways were dominated by neural and synaptic signaling, potassium channels, and cardiac conduction among other functions. The extracellular matrix and neural/synaptic signaling seem to be the main pathways of interest as they are the most strongly enriched in each direction with many overlapping genes affecting those pathways in coordination.

Comparing DAVID and fgsea results, both methods seemed to converge on the same conclusion which was an upregulation of extracellular matrix and secreted proteins, and a downregulation of synaptic and neural membrane genes. The agreement between the two methods with different methodologies strengthens confidence in these findings. The methods differed in detail as DAVID returned more broad annotation terms that describe protein features rather than pathways, whereas fgsea identified specific pathways. 

```{r deseq2}
# Run DESeq2
count_matrix <- counts_filtered %>% column_to_rownames("gene") %>% as.matrix()
sample_info <- coldata %>% column_to_rownames("sample")

dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(countData = count_matrix, colData = sample_info , design = ~ condition)
dds <-DESeq(dds)

res <- results(dds, contrast = c("condition", "exp", "control")) %>% as_tibble(rownames = "gene")
res
```

```{r top10_table}
# Table of the top 10 DE genes ranked by padj
top10_table <- res %>% arrange(padj) %>% head(10) %>% left_join(gene_map, by = join_by("gene" == "gene_id"))
top10_table
```

```{r significant_genes}
# Number of significant genes at your padj threshold, split into up- and downregulated
res_filtered <- res %>%
  filter(padj < 0.05)

#Count upregulated and downregulated genes
up <- sum(res_filtered$log2FoldChange > 0, na.rm = TRUE)
down <- sum(res_filtered$log2FoldChange < 0, na.rm = TRUE)

up
down
```

```{r enrichment_input}
# Prepare / write out gene lists and background for DAVID or Enrichr
# Upregulated genes: significant (padj < 0.05) and higher in exp than control
up_genes <- res_filtered %>%
  filter(log2FoldChange > 0) %>%
  left_join(gene_map, by = join_by(gene == gene_id))

# Downregulated genes: significant (padj < 0.05) and lower in exp than control
down_genes <- res_filtered %>%
  filter(log2FoldChange < 0) %>%
  left_join(gene_map, by = join_by(gene == gene_id))

# Background: every gene that was tested by DESeq2 (all genes that passed filtering)
background <- res %>%
  left_join(gene_map, by = join_by(gene == gene_id))

# Write gene names to separate text files, one name per line
write.table(unique(up_genes$gene_name), "up_genes.txt",
            quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE, col.names = FALSE)

write.table(unique(down_genes$gene_name), "down_genes.txt",
            quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE, col.names = FALSE)

write.table(unique(background$gene_name), "background.txt",
            quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE, col.names = FALSE)
```

## Sample Quality Control

Filtered counts were normalized using variance-stabilizing transformation (VST) with blind = TRUE. Principal component analysis showed that PC1 explained 86% of the variance and separated the samples by conditions: the three control samples clustering, while exp_rep1 and exp_rep2 grouped together on the opposite side of PC1. Exp_rep3 was positioned between the two groups on PC1 and was separated from all other samples along PC2, explaining, which explained the 10% of the variance. The sample-to-sample distance heatmap displayed the same pattern as well.

Overall the samples mostly clustered by group with the condition explaining the largest source of variation (control vs experimental). exp_rep3 was the least consistent sample and could be considered an outlier of the samples. With no covariates provided, no other sources of variation could be directly tested. Based on these plots, I would proceed with differential expression using all six samples as the main separation still seems to be driven by condition and removing the exp_rep3 would leave only 2 experimental replicates, reducing the ability to estimate variability within the group. With exp_rep3 being intermediate between the groups, it is likely to reduce the number of differentially expressed genes rather than introduce false positives which, in this case, is does not outweigh the cons of losing a replicate.

```{r normalize}
# Normalize the filtered counts (rlog or VST)
vsd <- vst(dds, blind = TRUE)
```

```{r pca}
# PCA biplot of PC1 vs. PC2 with sample information overlaid
plotPCA(vsd, intgroup = "condition")
```

```{r sample_distances}
# Heatmap or graphic of sample-to-sample distances
vsd_mat <- assay(vsd)
sample_dists <- dist(t(vsd_mat))
pheatmap(sample_dists %>% as.matrix())
```

## DAVID / Enrichr results



```{r fgsea}
# Run fgsea using C2 canonical pathways and log2 fold change as the ranking metric
# C2 canonical pathways (gene symbols) from MSigDB
c2_cp <- msigdbr(species = "Homo sapiens", category = "C2") %>%
  filter(str_detect(gs_subcat, "^CP"))

# Convert to the named list fgsea expects: pathway name -> vector of gene symbols
pathways <- split(c2_cp$gene_symbol, c2_cp$gs_name)
# Rank every tested gene by log2 fold change (exp vs control), named by gene symbol
ranked <- res %>%
  left_join(gene_map, by = join_by(gene == gene_id)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(log2FoldChange)) %>%
  distinct(gene_name, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  arrange(desc(log2FoldChange))

ranks <- ranked$log2FoldChange
names(ranks) <- ranked$gene_name
head(ranks)

set.seed(42)
fgsea_res <- fgsea(pathways = pathways, stats = ranks, minSize = 15, maxSize = 500) %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  arrange(padj)

fgsea_res
```

```{r fgsea_plot, fig.width = 11, fig.height = 7}
# Plot the top significantly enriched pathways
top_pathways <- fgsea_res %>%
  filter(padj < 0.05) %>%
  slice_head(n = 20)

ggplot(top_pathways, aes(x = NES, y = reorder(pathway, NES), fill = NES > 0)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "firebrick", "FALSE" = "steelblue"),
                    labels = c("TRUE" = "Up in exp", "FALSE" = "Down in exp"),
                    name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Top enriched C2 canonical pathways (fgsea, padj < 0.05)",
       x = "Normalized Enrichment Score (NES)",
       y = NULL)
```

## Comparing DAVID/Enrichr and fgsea
```{r david_results}
# DAVID Functional Annotation Chart results 
david_up <- read_csv("DAVIDChartReport_up_genes_2026-11-02.csv")
david_down <- read_csv("DAVIDChartReport_down_genes_2026-11-02.csv")

# keep terms with Benjamini-adjusted p < 0.05 (same cutoff as padj for DE genes)
david_up_sig <- david_up %>% filter(Benjamini < 0.05) %>% arrange(Benjamini)
david_down_sig <- david_down %>% filter(Benjamini < 0.05) %>% arrange(Benjamini)

# how many significant terms in each list
nrow(david_up_sig)
nrow(david_down_sig)

# top 10 terms
david_up_sig %>% select(Category, Term, Count, `Fold Enrichment`, Benjamini) %>% head(10)
david_down_sig %>% select(Category, Term, Count, `Fold Enrichment`, Benjamini) %>% head(10)
```



## Interpretations

The number of differentially expressed genes was 1,254 with 572 upregulated and 682 downregulated. With the PCA, 86% of the variance was explained by PC1 and separated samples by condition, indicating that the condition causes a large shift in expression. It seems the experimental condition shifts cells away from neural, synaptic, and developmental processes and more towards extracellular matrix and secretory processes. With these results, the experimental condition seems to reflect a change in cell state or in the cells' extracellular environment. 

The results that support the speculation the most are the DAVID and fgsea results as the two independent methods reached the same themes. For upregulated genes, DAVID extracellular matrix was 5.0-fold with a Benjamini value of 1.7e-23 while fgsea identified extracellular matrix organization and collagen formation among the top positively enriched pathways. For downregulated genes, DAVID synapse was 3.0-fold with a Benjamini value of 3.2e-13 while fgsea identified neuronal and synaptic signaling among the top negatively enriched pathways. The agreement provides further confidence in results as DAVID uses only the significant genes while fgsea uses every gene's fold change.


## Your Conclusions and Follow-up

### Validation experiments

1. qPCR on top DE genes: the idea would be to measure a few of the top upregulated genes and downregulated genes in new samples of each condition. With this, look to see if the upregulated genes are higher and downregulated genes are lower in experimental conditions with similar fold changes. If there seems to be no difference between groups or changes in opposite direction, this would suggeset teh RNA-seq findings are wrong.

2. Protein check: the idea would be to perform western blot for an extracellular matrix protein and synaptic protein. With this, look to see if protein levels change in the same direction as the RNA. If protein levels do not change, this would suggeset the RNA changes do not carry through to the protein level, weakening the speculated functional changes.

### Follow-up experiments

1. Different time points: take samples at several time points after the condition starts. The aim should be to see when the changes begin and whether downregulation or upregulation occurs before the other.
2. Functional assay: measure extracellular matrix deposition and neuronal function. The aim is to test whether the expression changes alter what the cells actually do.

## Introduction

The study revolves around Type 1 diabetes (T1D) as a chronic autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks and destroys insulin-producing pancreatic beta cells, eventually impairing the body's ability to regulate blood glucose. The gene TYK2, which encodes a Janus kinase involved in type I interferon signaling, has been associated with T1D susceptibility and plays an important role in immune responses. Notably, TYK2 variants that partially reduce its function are protective against T1D. However, its specific functions in pancreatic beta-cell development and responses to inflammation were not fully understood. The study was performed to investigate how TYK2 influences pancreatic beta-cell development, function, and responses to immune challenges, particularly to interferon-alpha. To investigate this, the authors generated TYK2 knockout human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) and differentiated them alongside wild-type cells into pancreatic islet-like cells (SC-islets), comparing the two genotypes at multiple stages of differentiation. The authors used bulk RNA sequencing, with three knockout and three wild-type replicates, to examine gene expression changes throughout pancreatic stem cell differentiation. They also used single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) to identify differences in gene expression among specific pancreatic cell populations. These bioinformatic techniques allowed the researchers to identify differentially expressed genes, examine developmental pathways, and investigate potential relationships between TYK2 and other genes such as KRAS and NEUROG3. Principal component analysis (PCA), gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA), and pathway enrichment analyses were also used to identify broader transcriptional patterns and biological processes affected by TYK2 loss. Together, these approaches helped determine how TYK2 regulates pancreatic endocrine development and interferon-induced immune responses, providing insight into its potential as a therapeutic target for T1D.

```{r volcano_plot}
# Volcano plot similar to figure 3C
volcano_df <- res %>%
  filter(!is.na(padj)) %>%
  left_join(gene_map, by = join_by(gene == gene_id)) %>%
  mutate(
    status = case_when(
      padj < 0.01 & log2FoldChange > 0 ~ "Up",
      padj < 0.01 & log2FoldChange < 0 ~ "Down",
      TRUE ~ "Not significant"
    ),
    neg_log10_p = -log10(pmax(pvalue, 1e-300))
  )

# Genes highlighted in the paper's figure 3C
label_genes <- c("KRAS", "LAMB2", "SPP1", "DUSP6", "SPRY2", "AKT3", "COL21A1", "APOE",
                 "KDR", "NEUROG3", "INSM1", "PAX6", "NEUROD1", "NKX2-2", "ONECUT1", "GABRB3")

top_labels <- volcano_df %>%
  filter(gene_name %in% label_genes)

ggplot(volcano_df, aes(x = log2FoldChange, y = neg_log10_p, color = status)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = top_labels, aes(label = gene_name),
                           size = 3, color = "black", max.overlaps = Inf) +
  annotate("text", x = -7, y = 290, label = "DOWN", color = "#00BFC4", size = 5) +
  annotate("text", x = 7, y = 290, label = "UP", color = "#F8766D", size = 5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Up" = "#F8766D", "Down" = "#00BFC4",
                                "Not significant" = "black")) +
  theme_classic() +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 15)) +
  labs(title = "Volcano plot: exp vs control (padj < 0.01)",
       x = "Expression difference (log2FC)",
       y = "Significance (-log10 p value)",
       color = NULL)
```

```{r figure_3f, fig.width=9, fig.height=8}
# Enrichment plot resembling figure 3F using your DAVID/Enrichr or fgsea results
pathway_cats <- c("KEGG_PATHWAY", "GOTERM_BP_DIRECT")

up_terms <- david_up_sig %>%
  filter(Category %in% pathway_cats) %>%
  arrange(Benjamini) %>%
  head(8) %>%
  mutate(direction = "up")

down_terms <- david_down_sig %>%
  filter(Category %in% pathway_cats) %>%
  arrange(Benjamini) %>%
  head(8) %>%
  mutate(direction = "down")

fig3f_df <- bind_rows(up_terms, down_terms) %>%
  mutate(percent = Count / `Pop Hits` * 100,
         direction = factor(direction, levels = c("up", "down")))  # up panel on top

ggplot(fig3f_df, aes(x = percent, y = reorder(Term, percent), fill = Benjamini)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_grid(direction ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y",
             labeller = as_labeller(c(up = "\u2191", down = "\u2193"))) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "red", high = "blue") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0, size = 16),  # upright arrows
        strip.background = element_blank()) +              # no box around arrows
  labs(title = "Enrichment (DAVID KEGG + GO BP)", fill = "Adjusted p value",
       x = "Percentage of DE genes in category / all genes in category (%)",
       y = NULL)
```

### 1. Up- and downregulated genes

At padj < 0.01, differentially expressed genes were found to be 332 upregulated and 403 downregulated while the paper reported 319 upregulated and 412 downregulated. The difference between my findings and the paper's reportings is 13 more upregulated genes and 9 fewer downregulated genes, with a total of 735 genes in my findings and 731 in the paper's. Both analyses found more downregulated than upregulated genes, and the counts agree closely despite differences in the two pipelines.  

```{r compare_counts}
# Number of up- and downregulated genes at the authors' significance threshold
paper_res_filtered <- res %>%
  filter(padj < 0.01)

#Count upregulated and downregulated genes
up_01 <- sum(paper_res_filtered$log2FoldChange > 0, na.rm = TRUE)
down_01 <- sum(paper_res_filtered$log2FoldChange < 0, na.rm = TRUE)

up_01
down_01
```

### 2. Enrichment comparison

The authors reported upregulation of extracellular matrix organization, integrin cell surface interactions, extracellular matrix proteoglycans, and signaling by receptor tyrosine kinases while reporting downregulation of beta-cell development, neuronal system, and regulation of gene expression in beta cells. Overall my findings agree with these results. Upregulated genes were enriched for extracellular matrix in both DAVID and fgsea. Downregulated genes were enriched for neural and synaptic functions in both DAVID and fgsea as well. DAVID also identified PI3K-Akt signaling among the upregulated genes, which acts downstream of receptor tyrosine kinases. 

There were also some key differences as the beta-cell signal was weaker in my results. Maturity onset diabetes of the young was the only clearly beta-cell-related term, and no beta-cell pathways appeared among the top fgsea results. My results also included terms not reported by the authors such as p53 signaling and cytochrome P450 drug metabolism among the upregulated genes. These differences seem to be caused, in part, by the different databases used as the authors used Reactome, while my analyses used DAVID's KEGG and GO terms and MSigDB canonical pathways for fgsea, so pathway names do not match exactly.

## Comparing Interpretations

> **Instructions (2-3 paragraphs):** Return to your first interpretations about the major
> biological pathways implicated in the results:
>
> - Did the authors emphasize any genes or pathways that were weak or absent in your
>   results? How strongly do you think their data support those claims?
> - Which of your findings agree with the authors'? Does reaching the same result through
